Surat al-Lahab is Meccan and has five verses.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he.﴾ ﴿His wealth and what he gained will not avail him.﴾ ﴿He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame.﴾ ﴿And his wife, the carrier of firewood.﴾ ﴿Around her neck is a rope of palm fiber.﴾

Al-hatab (الحَطَبُ) means firewood. It is said: "So-and-so yahtibu (يَحْطِبُ) against so-and-so," when he informs on him. Al-jid (الجِيدُ) means the neck. Al-masad (المَسَدُ) means a rope made of palm fiber. Abu al-Fath said: it is the fiber of the doum palm. Ibn Zayd said: it is a tree in Yemen called al-masad. End quote. It may also be made from camel hides or camel hair. The rajaz poet said:

"And a masad of the ropes of she-camels."

A man described as mamsud al-khalq means he is tightly woven and firmly built.

﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he.﴾ ﴿His wealth and what he gained will not avail him.﴾ ﴿He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame.﴾ ﴿And his wife, the carrier of firewood.﴾ ﴿Around her neck is a rope of palm fiber.﴾

[p. 525] This surah is Meccan. When the previous passage mentioned people entering the religion of God, the Exalted, it followed with mention of those who did not enter the religion and who lost out by not entering what the people of Mecca had entered of faith. The discussion of tabab (التَّبابُ, ruin) was given earlier in Surat Ghafir. Here, Ibn Abbas said: "kharabat" (she was ruined); Qatadah said: "khasirat" (she lost); Ibn Jubayr said: "halakat" (she perished); Ata said: "dallat" (she went astray); Yaman ibn Riyab said: "safirat" (she was emptied of all good). These statements are close in meaning. They also said, as transmitted: "Ashabbatun am tabbatun?" meaning: is she destroyed by old age and incapacity? The attribution of destruction to the two hands is because most work is done by them, though in reality it belongs to the person himself, as in His saying: ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forward﴾ (Surah al-Hajj, 22:10). It was also said that he took a stone in his hands to throw at the Messenger ﷺ, so tabb was attributed to the hands. Apparently, tabb (تَبَّ) is a supplication, and tabba (تَبَّ) as a verb is an announcement that this has occurred, as the poet said:

"He rewarded me, may God reward him with the worst of his rewards, the reward of rabid dogs, and he has indeed done so."

This is supported by the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud): "wa qad tabba" (and he has indeed perished). It is narrated that when the verse ﴿And warn your closest kinsmen﴾ (Surat al-Shu'ara, 26:214) was revealed, he (ﷺ) said: "O Safiyyah bint Abd al-Muttalib, O Fatimah bint Muhammad, I cannot avail you anything against God. Ask me for whatever you wish from my wealth." Then he ascended al-Safa and called out to the clans of Quraysh: "O Banu so-and-so, O Banu so-and-so." It is also narrated that he shouted at the top of his voice: "Yaa sabahaah!" They gathered to him from every direction, and he said to them: "Tell me, if I told you that horsemen were about to attack you at the foot of this mountain, would you believe me?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment." Abu Lahab said: "May you perish for the whole day! Is this why you gathered us?" The people dispersed from him, and this surah was revealed.

Abu Lahab's name was Abd al-Uzza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the paternal uncle of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Kathir read ﴿Abi Lahab﴾ with the ha' (هَ) sukun (silent). The rest of the seven readers vocalized it with a fatha. They did not differ on ﴿dhata lahab﴾ because it is a fasila (فاصِلَة, verse-ending rhyme), and sukun would destroy the beauty of the fasila. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is a case of changing proper names, like their saying "Shums Malik" with a damma. End quote. He means the sukun of the ha' in Lahb and the damma of the shin in Shums, and he means in the poet's words:

"I am indeed praising, aiming with it at my cousin, the truthful one, Shums ibn Malik."

As for Lahab, the well-known vocalization of his kunya is with a fatha on the ha'. As for Shums ibn Malik, it is not necessarily a case of changing proper names; it could be a name taken from the plural form shums, as in the phrase "adhnabu khayl shums" (tails of horses that are...). It was said that he was given the kunya Abu Lahab because of his beauty and the brightness of his face. God did not mention him by name because his name was Abd al-Uzza, so He turned away from it to the kunya. Or because the kunya was more prevalent for him than his name. Or because his end would be the Fire, so his condition matched his kunya, just as one says to a wicked person "Abu al-Sharr" (father of evil) and to a good person "Abu al-Khayr" (father of good). Or because the name is nobler than the kunya, so He turned to the less noble form. For this reason God mentioned the prophets, peace be upon them, by their names and did not give any of them a kunya.

Apparently, the mā (ما) in ﴿mā aghnā ʿanhu māluhu﴾ is a negation, meaning his wealth inherited from his fathers did not avail him. ﴿wa mā kasab﴾ (and what he gained) refers to himself, or to his livestock and what he gained from their offspring and benefits, or what he gained from the profits of his wealth with which he traded. It is permissible for the mā in ﴿mā aghnā﴾ to be an interrogative in a position of accusative, meaning: "What thing will his wealth avail him?" as an affirmation and denial. The meaning would be: where is the wealth and gain that belonged to him? Apparently, the mā in His saying ﴿wa mā kasab﴾ is a relative pronoun. It was also permitted that it be a verbal noun (maṣdariyya). If the mā in ﴿mā aghnā﴾ is interrogative, the mā in ﴿wa mā kasab﴾ may also be interrogative, meaning: "And what did he gain?" That is, he gained nothing. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that ﴿wa mā kasab﴾ refers to his son.

In a hadith: "A man's child is from his earnings." It is narrated from al-Dahhak that ﴿wa mā kasab﴾ is his wicked deed against the Messenger ﷺ. From Qatadah: and his deed which he thought was of some benefit. It is narrated from him that he used to say: "If what my nephew says is true, I will ransom myself from it with my wealth and my children."

Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) read: "wa mā iktasab" with the ta' of the iftiʿal form (افْتِعال, a verbal pattern). Abu Hayawa, Ibn Miqsam, and Abbas (in his choice of reading) read ﴿sa-yuṣlā﴾ with a damma on the ya', fatha on the sad, and shadda on the lam. It was also read "Muraʾatuhu" and from him also "Muraiyyatuhu" in diminutive form, with hamza and with replacing it with ya' and merging the ya' of diminutive with the ya' [p. 526] in it. He also read: "ḥammālatun lil-ḥaṭab" with tanwin on ḥammālatun and the lam of the genitive on al-ḥaṭab. Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿sa-yaṣlā﴾ with a damma on the ya' and sukun on the sad. Abu Qilabah read "ḥāmilatu al-ḥaṭab" in the pattern fā'ilah, in construct. Abu Amr in one transmission, al-Hasan, Zayd ibn Ali, al-A'raj, Abu Hayawa, Ibn Abi Ablah, Ibn Muhaysin, and Asim read ﴿ḥammālata﴾ in the accusative, and they shortened the vowel of the ha' in "wa-imra'atuhu."

The majority read ﴿sa-yaṣlā﴾ with a fatha on the ya' and sukun on the sad; "wa-imra'atuhu" in the nominative; and ﴿ḥammālata﴾ in the pattern fa''āla for intensification, in construct with al-ḥaṭab in the nominative. The sin (س) indicates the future, even if the time is delayed, and this is a threat that will certainly be carried out. "Wa-imra'atuhu" is in the nominative as a conjunction upon the pronoun concealed in ﴿sa-yaṣlā﴾, and what made it acceptable was the separation by the object and its modifier. In the reading of the majority, ḥammālatu is the predicate of a deleted subject, or an adjective of "imra'atuhu," because it is a past pattern and is therefore definite through the construct. Fa''āl is one of the six patterns, and its rule is like that of the active participle. In the reading with the accusative, it is in the accusative as a form of censure. In the reading with the nominative, they permitted "wa-imra'atuhu" to be the subject, and ḥammālata with its noun, Umm Jamil bint Harb, the sister of Abu Sufyan. She was blind in one eye. Apparently she used to carry firewood, meaning that which has thorns, to hurt the Messenger ﷺ and his companions by throwing it on their path to wound them. For this she was blamed and called "the carrier of firewood," as Ibn Abbas said. So ḥammālatun is definite. If it became her epithet, it is permissible in the nominative case for it to be an appositive (ʿaṭf bayān) or a substitute (badal). It was said: she used to carry a bundle of thorns, thistle, and sa'dan, and spread it at night on the path of the Messenger of God ﷺ. Ibn Abbas also said, with Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Suddi: she used to walk about carrying tales (namima). It is said of one who carries tales: "he carries firewood among the people," meaning he kindles strife among them and causes evil. The poet said:

"Of the fair women who have not hunted on the back of a mare, and have not walked among the tribe with green firewood."

He made it green to indicate the smoke, which is an increase in evil. The rajaz poet said:

"Indeed the sons of al-Arzam are carriers of firewood; they are the tale-bearers in contentment and in anger."

Ibn Jubayr said: "carrier of sins and offenses," from their saying "yahtibu ʿalā ẓahrihi" (he carries on his back). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿and they bear their burdens upon their backs﴾ (Surat al-An'am, 6:31). It was also said: al-hatab is the plural of hatib, like ḥāris and ḥaras, meaning bringing the criminals to their crimes. The apparent meaning of al-ḥabl min masad is that the rope is of palm fiber. ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, and Sufyan said: it is a metaphor, and what is meant is a chain of iron in Hell. Qatadah said: a necklace of ward (a kind of shell or bead). Ibn al-Musayyib said: a precious necklace of jewels. She said: "By al-Lat and al-Uzza, I will spend it on enmity against Muhammad." Ibn Atiyyah said: He described her necklace as a rope of palm fiber only as a sign of ill omen for her, and to mention her adornment in this wicked endeavor. End quote. Al-Hasan said: it was only beads. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is that around her neck is a rope of ropes, and she carries a bundle of thorns and ties it around her neck, as the woodcutters do, to humiliate and belittle her, by making her appear like some of the women who gather firewood, so that she and her husband would be humiliated, though they were in the house of honor and nobility, and in a position of wealth and prosperity. Some people insulted al-Fadl ibn al-Abbas ibn Utbah ibn Abi Lahab with "carrier of firewood," and he said:

"What have you intended by insulting me and by disparaging me, or by reproaching me for the carrier of firewood?

A woman of great beauty, lofty in glory, who was the daughter of a shaykh of ancient and noble lineage."

It may be that the meaning is: her condition will be in the Fire of Hell in the form she had when she carried the bundle of thorns. So there will always be on her back a bundle of firewood of the Zaqqum tree or of the dari', and around her neck a rope made of the chains of the Fire, just as every criminal is punished with that which matches his crime. End quote. When Umm Jamil heard this surah, she came to Abu Bakr while he was with the Messenger of God ﷺ in the mosque, holding a stone in her hand. She said: "It has reached me that your companion has satirized me. By God, I will do such and such." God the Exalted blinded her sight to the Messenger of God ﷺ. It is narrated that Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, said to her: "Do you see anyone with me?" She said: "Are you mocking me? I see no one but you. And if he is a poet, then I am like him," and she recited:

"We have disobeyed Mudhammam (dispraised one), and we have rejected his religion, and we have disobeyed his command."

Abu Bakr remained silent and she departed. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Angels screened me from her, so she did not see me, and God sufficed against her evil." It is mentioned that she died strangled by her rope. Abu Lahab, God struck him with the plague (ʿadasa) seven nights after the Battle of Badr.

Here, Ibn Abbas said: "kharabat" (she was ruined); Qatadah said: "khasirat" (she lost); Ibn Jubayr said: "halakat" (she perished); Ata said: "dallat" (she went astray); Yaman ibn Riyab said: "safirat" (she was emptied of all good). These statements are close in meaning. They also said, as transmitted: "Ashabbatun am tabbatun?" meaning: is she destroyed by old age and incapacity? The attribution of destruction to the two hands is because most work is done by them, though in reality it belongs to the person himself, as in His saying: ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forward﴾ (Surah al-Hajj, 22:10). It was also said that he took a stone in his hands to throw at the Messenger ﷺ, so tabb was attributed to the hands. Apparently, tabb (تَبَّ) is a supplication, and tabba (تَبَّ) as a verb is an announcement that this has occurred, as the poet said:

"He rewarded me, may God reward him with the worst of his rewards, the reward of rabid dogs, and he has indeed done so."

This is supported by the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud): "wa qad tabba" (and he has indeed perished). It is narrated that when the verse ﴿And warn your closest kinsmen﴾ (Surat al-Shu'ara, 26:214) was revealed, he (ﷺ) said: "O Safiyyah bint Abd al-Muttalib, O Fatimah bint Muhammad, I cannot avail you anything against God. Ask me for whatever you wish from my wealth." Then he ascended al-Safa and called out to the clans of Quraysh: "O Banu so-and-so, O Banu so-and-so." It is also narrated that he shouted at the top of his voice: "Yaa sabahaah!" They gathered to him from every direction, and he said to them: "Tell me, if I told you that horsemen were about to attack you at the foot of this mountain, would you believe me?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment." Abu Lahab said: "May you perish for the whole day! Is this why you gathered us?" The people dispersed from him, and this surah was revealed.

Abu Lahab's name was Abd al-Uzza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the paternal uncle of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Kathir read ﴿Abi Lahab﴾ with the ha' (هَ) sukun (silent). The rest of the seven readers vocalized it with a fatha. They did not differ on ﴿dhata lahab﴾ because it is a fasila (فاصِلَة, verse-ending rhyme), and sukun would destroy the beauty of the fasila. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is a case of changing proper names, like their saying "Shums Malik" with a damma. End quote. He means the sukun of the ha' in Lahb and the damma of the shin in Shums, and he means in the poet's words:

"I am indeed praising, aiming with it at my cousin, the truthful one, Shums ibn Malik."

As for Lahab, the well-known vocalization of his kunya is with a fatha on the ha'. As for Shums ibn Malik, it is not necessarily a case of changing proper names; it could be a name taken from the plural form shums, as in the phrase "adhnabu khayl shums" (tails of horses that are...). It was said that he was given the kunya Abu Lahab because of his beauty and the brightness of his face. God did not mention him by name because his name was Abd al-Uzza, so He turned away from it to the kunya. Or because the kunya was more prevalent for him than his name. Or because his end would be the Fire, so his condition matched his kunya, just as one says to a wicked person "Abu al-Sharr" (father of evil) and to a good person "Abu al-Khayr" (father of good). Or because the name is nobler than the kunya, so He turned to the less noble form. For this reason God mentioned the prophets, peace be upon them, by their names and did not give any of them a kunya.

Apparently, the mā (ما) in ﴿mā aghnā ʿanhu māluhu﴾ is a negation, meaning his wealth inherited from his fathers did not avail him. ﴿wa mā kasab﴾ (and what he gained) refers to himself, or to his livestock and what he gained from their offspring and benefits, or what he gained from the profits of his wealth with which he traded. It is permissible for the mā in ﴿mā aghnā﴾ to be an interrogative in a position of accusative, meaning: "What thing will his wealth avail him?" as an affirmation and denial. The meaning would be: where is the wealth and gain that belonged to him? Apparently, the mā in His saying ﴿wa mā kasab﴾ is a relative pronoun. It was also permitted that it be a verbal noun (maṣdariyya). If the mā in ﴿mā aghnā﴾ is interrogative, the mā in ﴿wa mā kasab﴾ may also be interrogative, meaning: "And what did he gain?" That is, he gained nothing. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that ﴿wa mā kasab﴾ refers to his son.

In a hadith: "A man's child is from his earnings." It is narrated from al-Dahhak that ﴿wa mā kasab﴾ is his wicked deed against the Messenger ﷺ. From Qatadah: and his deed which he thought was of some benefit. It is narrated from him that he used to say: "If what my nephew says is true, I will ransom myself from it with my wealth and my children."

Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) read: "wa mā iktasab" with the ta' of the iftiʿal form (افْتِعال, a verbal pattern). Abu Hayawa, Ibn Miqsam, and Abbas (in his choice of reading) read ﴿sa-yuṣlā﴾ with a damma on the ya', fatha on the sad, and shadda on the lam. It was also read "Muraʾatuhu" and from him also "Muraiyyatuhu" in diminutive form, with hamza and with replacing it with ya' and merging the ya' of diminutive with the ya' [p. 526] in it. He also read: "ḥammālatun lil-ḥaṭab" with tanwin on ḥammālatun and the lam of the genitive on al-ḥaṭab. Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿sa-yaṣlā﴾ with a damma on the ya' and sukun on the sad. Abu Qilabah read "ḥāmilatu al-ḥaṭab" in the pattern fā'ilah, in construct. Abu Amr in one transmission, al-Hasan, Zayd ibn Ali, al-A'raj, Abu Hayawa, Ibn Abi Ablah, Ibn Muhaysin, and Asim read ﴿ḥammālata﴾ in the accusative, and they shortened the vowel of the ha' in "wa-imra'atuhu."

The majority read ﴿sa-yaṣlā﴾ with a fatha on the ya' and sukun on the sad; "wa-imra'atuhu" in the nominative; and ﴿ḥammālata﴾ in the pattern fa''āla for intensification, in construct with al-ḥaṭab in the nominative. The sin (س) indicates the future, even if the time is delayed, and this is a threat that will certainly be carried out. "Wa-imra'atuhu" is in the nominative as a conjunction upon the pronoun concealed in ﴿sa-yaṣlā﴾, and what made it acceptable was the separation by the object and its modifier. In the reading of the majority, ḥammālatu is the predicate of a deleted subject, or an adjective of "imra'atuhu," because it is a past pattern and is therefore definite through the construct. Fa''āl is one of the six patterns, and its rule is like that of the active participle. In the reading with the accusative, it is in the accusative as a form of censure. In the reading with the nominative, they permitted "wa-imra'atuhu" to be the subject, and ḥammālata with its noun, Umm Jamil bint Harb, the sister of Abu Sufyan. She was blind in one eye. Apparently she used to carry firewood, meaning that which has thorns, to hurt the Messenger ﷺ and his companions by throwing it on their path to wound them. For this she was blamed and called "the carrier of firewood," as Ibn Abbas said. So ḥammālatun is definite. If it became her epithet, it is permissible in the nominative case for it to be an appositive (ʿaṭf bayān) or a substitute (badal). It was said: she used to carry a bundle of thorns, thistle, and sa'dan, and spread it at night on the path of the Messenger of God ﷺ. Ibn Abbas also said, with Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Suddi: she used to walk about carrying tales (namima). It is said of one who carries tales: "he carries firewood among the people," meaning he kindles strife among them and causes evil. The poet said:

"Of the fair women who have not hunted on the back of a mare, and have not walked among the tribe with green firewood."

He made it green to indicate the smoke, which is an increase in evil. The rajaz poet said:

"Indeed the sons of al-Arzam are carriers of firewood; they are the tale-bearers in contentment and in anger."

Ibn Jubayr said: "carrier of sins and offenses," from their saying "yahtibu ʿalā ẓahrihi" (he carries on his back). God, the Exalted, said: ﴿and they bear their burdens upon their backs﴾ (Surat al-An'am, 6:31). It was also said: al-hatab is the plural of hatib, like ḥāris and ḥaras, meaning bringing the criminals to their crimes. The apparent meaning of al-ḥabl min masad is that the rope is of palm fiber. ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, and Sufyan said: it is a metaphor, and what is meant is a chain of iron in Hell. Qatadah said: a necklace of ward (a kind of shell or bead). Ibn al-Musayyib said: a precious necklace of jewels. She said: "By al-Lat and al-Uzza, I will spend it on enmity against Muhammad." Ibn Atiyyah said: He described her necklace as a rope of palm fiber only as a sign of ill omen for her, and to mention her adornment in this wicked endeavor. End quote. Al-Hasan said: it was only beads. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is that around her neck is a rope of ropes, and she carries a bundle of thorns and ties it around her neck, as the woodcutters do, to humiliate and belittle her, by making her appear like some of the women who gather firewood, so that she and her husband would be humiliated, though they were in the house of honor and nobility, and in a position of wealth and prosperity. Some people insulted al-Fadl ibn al-Abbas ibn Utbah ibn Abi Lahab with "carrier of firewood," and he said:

"What have you intended by insulting me and by disparaging me, or by reproaching me for the carrier of firewood?

A woman of great beauty, lofty in glory, who was the daughter of a shaykh of ancient and noble lineage."

It may be that the meaning is: her condition will be in the Fire of Hell in the form she had when she carried the bundle of thorns. So there will always be on her back a bundle of firewood of the Zaqqum tree or of the dari', and around her neck a rope made of the chains of the Fire, just as every criminal is punished with that which matches his crime. End quote. When Umm Jamil heard this surah, she came to Abu Bakr while he was with the Messenger of God ﷺ in the mosque, holding a stone in her hand. She said: "It has reached me that your companion has satirized me. By God, I will do such and such." God the Exalted blinded her sight to the Messenger of God ﷺ. It is narrated that Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, said to her: "Do you see anyone with me?" She said: "Are you mocking me? I see no one but you. And if he is a poet, then I am like him," and she recited:

"We have disobeyed Mudhammam (dispraised one), and we have rejected his religion, and we have disobeyed his command."

Abu Bakr remained silent and she departed. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Angels screened me from her, so she did not see me, and God sufficed against her evil." It is mentioned that she died strangled by her rope. Abu Lahab, God struck him with the plague (ʿadasa) seven nights after the Battle of Badr.
